Finally, baicalin increases HDAC1 protein levels to inhibit H3K9 lactylation-mediated microglial M1 polarization via targeting AMPKα1. Conclusion These findings suggest that, when administered at an early stage after HIE, baicalin may contribute to the attenuation of HIE pathology, at least in part by increasing HDAC1 stability through AMPKα1- and UBE3A-mediated "phosphorylation-ubiquitination hierarchical regulation", thereby reducing H3K9 lactylation and suppressing microglial M1 polarization.

title: Multi-omics integrated analysis reveals the therapeutic mechanism of 919 formula in metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease
abstract: Background Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is the most prevalent chronic liver disease worldwide and is driven by metabolic stress-induced inflammation. Emerging evidence implicates cytotoxic CD8⁺ T cells as key contributors to the progression of MASLD. However, therapeutic strategies specifically targeting pathogenic CD8⁺ T cell responses in MASLD are still scarce. The clinical efficacy of the 919 formula in MASLD has been demonstrated, yet its cellular targets and molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Methods Single-cell transcriptomics profiled peripheral blood immune composition in 919 formula treated MASLD patients, and UPLC-QE-MS characterized bioactive constituents of the 919 formula. Efficacy and immune mechanisms were tested in HFD/MCD mouse models (AST/ALT and histology) and CD8⁺ T cell adoptive transfer. CD8⁺ T cells treated with control or 919 formula-containing serum were analyzed by flow cytometry, Seahorse assays, transcriptomics, immunoblotting, and molecular docking. Results Single-cell transcriptomic profiling showed that 919 formula treatment was associated with a selective reduction in circulating CD8⁺ GZMB⁺ T cells and an attenuation of CD8⁺ T-cell activation in patients with MASLD. In both HFD- and MCD-induced mouse models, the 919 formula markedly alleviated hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis, which was accompanied by a decreased proportion of CD8⁺ GZMB⁺ T cells, reflecting reduced CD8⁺ T-cell activation. Furthermore, adoptive transfer experiments demonstrated that CD8⁺ T cells treated with 919 formula-containing serum were sufficient to confer protection against MCD-induced liver injury. Mechanistically, 919 formula treatment was associated with reduced PKM2-dependent glycolysis and STAT5 phosphorylation in CD8⁺ T cells, while pharmacological activation of PKM2 partially reversed these effects. Finally, Schizandrin C was identified as a representative bioactive component of the 919 formula. Molecular docking and SPR analyses supported its direct interaction with PKM2, while functional assays demonstrated its capacity to suppress CD8⁺ T-cell activation. Conclusion Together, these findings suggest that the 919 formula alleviates MASLD, at least in part, by attenuating pathological CD8⁺ T-cell activation and cytotoxicity, with PKM2-STAT5 signaling potentially contributing to this effect. Schizandrin C may contribute to the therapeutic effects of the 919 formula, although the overall efficacy of this complex herbal formulation is likely to involve coordinated actions of multiple bioactive constituents.

title: Caragana sinica root bioactive fraction ameliorates experimental arthritis by inhibiting synovial inflammatory lesions through targeting HSP90α
abstract: Background Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease with synovial inflammatory lesions as the initiating factor and pivotal pathogenic driver, triggering persistent inflammation and progressive joint destruction. While Caragana sinica root has long been used in folk medicine for rheumatic disorders, its specific bioactive fractions and therapeutic mechanisms in RA remain unelucidated. Objective This study aims to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of the bioactive fraction from Caragana sinica root (CSRBF) against experimental arthritis and clarify its underlying mechanism by identifying core targets and exploring its regulatory effects on fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLSs). Method CSRBF was prepared via 70% ethanol reflux extraction and macroporous resin purification. Adjuvant-induced arthritis (AA) rats model and TNF-α-stimulated FLSs were used to evaluate CSRBF's efficacy. In vivo therapeutic effects were assessed via arthritis index scoring, histological staining, gait analysis, and micro-CT. In vitro, cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and pro-inflammatory cytokine expression were detected. Core targets were identified and verified using LiP-MS, LC-MS, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and CETSA. Result CSRBF dose-dependently alleviated AA severity in rats, reduced synovial hyperplasia, cartilage erosion, and bone destruction, while improving motor function. In vitro, CSRBF inhibited TNF-α-induced FLSs proliferation, migration, invasion, and excessive secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines. HSP90α was confirmed as the core target of CSRBF, with three active components (hesperetin, pinocembrin, and secoisolariciresinol) directly binding to HSP90α. Conclusion CSRBF ameliorates experimental arthritis by targeting HSP90α to inhibit FLSs-mediated synovial inflammation, highlighting it as a promising natural anti-RA candidate and HSP90α as a valuable therapeutic target.

title: Qishen granule improves myocardial fibrosis in heart failure via Piezo1/Calpain2/LAMP1/CTSS in CCR2+ macrophages
abstract: Background Myocardial fibrosis represents a common terminal pathological pathway in heart failure (HF), and currently, there is a lack of therapies specifically targeting the core pathological mechanisms of myocardial fibrosis, namely persistent inflammation and excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition. In the present study, our aim was to evaluate the effectiveness of the herbal formulation Qishen Granule (QSG) against myocardial fibrosis. Methods A model of HF with myocardial fibrosis was established by performing left anterior descending artery (LAD) ligation in mice. After three weeks of QSG treatment, cardiac function, fibrosis, and cardiac conduction were evaluated. We identified potential targets through network pharmacology and RNA sequencing analysis. The targeted effects of QSG were further validated using flow cytometry, Western blot, quantitative real-time PCR, and immunofluorescence techniques. Results QSG can improve the heart function of HF mice, reduce myocardial inflammation and fibrosis, and effectively enhance cardiac conduction function. Its core mechanism lies in regulating the mechanosensitive ion channel Piezo1 and the calcium-dependent cysteine protease 2 (Calpain2) activation cascade, thereby blocking lysosome-associated membrane protein 1 (LAMP1) hydrolysis and cathepsin S (CTSS) release while reducing ECM deposition. In CCR2 + macrophages, QSG inhibits calcium influx by reducing Piezo1 expression, thereby suppressing myofibroblast activation. Knockdown of Piezo1 partially abrogates QSG's antifibrotic effects, confirming Piezo1 as an essential target for QSG's protective actions. Conclusions QSG reduces ECM deposition by targeting and inhibiting the Piezo1/Calpain2/LAMP1/CTSS signal axis in CCR2 + macrophages, thus improving myocardial fibrosis. This study provides a novel therapeutic strategy for HF-associated myocardial fibrosis by leveraging mechanosensitive signaling pathways.

title: Gastrodia elata Blume-derived exosomes-like nanovesicles deliver miR-221-3p and miR-222-3p to ameliorate doxorubicin cardiotoxicity
abstract: Background and purpose The widely used antitumor drug doxorubicin (DOX) is clinically limited because of its tendency to induce cardiotoxicity, and there is currently no optimal protection strategy. Plant-derived exosomes-like nanovesicles have shown potential for treating a variety of diseases. Here, we report the therapeutic effects of Gastrodia elata Blume-derived exosomes-like nanovesicles (GE-ELNs) in mitigating DOX cardiotoxicity and explore the underlying mechanisms. Methods and results GE-ELNs exhibited a typical morphology and size consistent with mammalian exosomes and were enriched in RNA, proteins, and lipids. In vivo IVIS imaging confirmed the recruitment of GE-ELNs to the heart after intravenous injection. Fluorescence microcopy and flow cytometry analysis revealed a time and dose-dependent increase in the uptake of GE-ELNs by cardiomyocytes. While GE-ELNs treatment decreased apoptosis and restored calcium transients in DOX-treated cardiomyocytes, it did not significantly affect the toxicity of DOX in several breast cancer cell lines. In a rat model of acute DOX cardiotoxicity, GE-ELNs mitigated cardiotoxicity and improved left ventricular function and cardiac structure. Similar protective effects were also observed in BALB/c mice with implanted breast cancer xenografts without promoting tumor growth or metastasis or comprising the antitumor efficiency of DOX. Mechanistic studies using RNA sequencing and miRNA mimics/inhibitor transfection revealed that miR-221-3p and miR-222-3p are key factors that mediate the protective effects of GE-ELNs. Conclusions Collectively, our study revealed that while GE-ELNs attenuated DOX cardiotoxicity, they had very limited effects on the survival of cancer cells and tumor growth. GE-ELNs may represent a novel therapeutic approach to prevent DOX cardiotoxicity.

title: Levistilide A alleviates pulmonary fibrosis by blocking the cation channel PIEZO1-centered signaling pathway in fibroblasts
abstract: Background Pulmonary fibrosis (PF) is a common pathological feature of various chronic lung diseases, characterized by destruction of lung parenchyma and alveolar structure, aberrant angiogenesis and fibroblast proliferation. Therefore, determining the main contributing factors of PF and finding effective targeted medications are an urgent concern that needs to be resolved. This study investigated the pharmacological mechanisms on therapeutic effects of levistilide A (LevA) for PF. Methods Bleomycin (BLM)-induced PF mice and mice fibroblast cell line L929 cells were used to investigate the inhibitory effect of LevA on calcium signaling-mediated angiogenesis and fibroblast growth, and explain its underlying mechanism by the RNA-sequencing analysis, the protein-protein interactions and the gene functional correlation analysis, as well as molecular biology experiments. Results We first demonstrated that PIEZO1 was enhanced in the lungs of PF patients and mouse models and strongly associated with angiogenesis and fibroblast proliferation. Notably, LevA remarkably improved BLM-induced PF by suppressing the cation channel PIEZO1 and calcium signaling in fibroblasts, which reduced the CAMKK2/CAMK1/p-CREB/HIF-1α/VEGF pathway-mediated angiogenesis, as well as the CALPAIN2/WNT/β-CATENIN pathway-linked fibroblast growth. According to our in vitro and in vivo studies, the continuous activation of PIEZO1 counteracted the therapeutic benefits of LevA. Mechanically, LevA directly bound to and promoted K63-linked polyubiquitination and subsequent degradation of PIEZO1 in fibroblasts via interaction with the E3 ligase TRIM25. Conclusion LevA ameliorates PF via inhibiting PIEZO1 and calcium signaling-centered angiogenesis and fibroblast proliferation pathways. This study provides a new scientific foundation and perspective for PF therapy.

title: Editorial: 8th International Symposium on Phytochemicals in Medicine and Food
Aqueous extract of Paeoniae Radix Alba alleviates DSS-induced ulcerative colitis via inhibition of the IFN-γ/JAK1/STAT1 signaling pathway and restoration of intestinal barrier function
abstract: BACKGROUND: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by aberrant immune activation and intestinal microenvironment dysregulation. Paeoniae Radix Alba (RPA), a classic traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) derived from the roots of Paeonia lactiflora, possesses potent anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, and analgesic properties. It has been extensively employed in traditional Chinese prescriptions for the treatment of UC. However, the precise mechanism underlying its beneficial effects in alleviating UC pathology remains to be clearly elucidated. PURPOSE: We explored the regulatory effects of the aqueous extract of RPA (hereafter termed RPAE) on the Janus kinase 1 (JAK1)/signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1) signaling pathway and intestinal barrier integrity, to clarify the potential mechanisms by which RPAE alleviates UC progression. METHODS: The constituents of RPAE were identified by UPLC-Q-Orbitrap-MS. Its therapeutic efficacy was evaluated in a dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)-induced UC mouse model by the following parameters: disease activity index (DAI), colon length, colonic histopathology, and inflammatory cytokine levels [Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and qRT-PCR] in serum and colonic tissues. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) were used to visualize colonic damage. Fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC)-dextran assay assessed intestinal barrier integrity. Furthermore, transcriptomics analysis was conducted to explore the potential molecular mechanism, and the key pathways were verified in a lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced inflammatory model established in RAW 264.7 macrophages. RESULTS: A total of 51 components were identified in RPAE, among which monoterpene glycosides were predominant. In vivo experiments demonstrated that RPAE ameliorated the UC-associated symptoms in mice, including body weight loss, colon shortening, and elevated DAI scores. Moreover, RPAE regulated the secretion of TNF-α, IL-1β, IFN-γ, and IL-10 in the serum and colon tissues of UC mice. Histopathological examination further confirmed that RPAE treatment ameliorated colon tissue damage and markedly upregulated the expression of ZO-1 and Occludin, thereby preserving intestinal barrier integrity. Transcriptomic bioinformatic analysis revealed significant enrichment of differentially expressed genes in the JAK-STAT signaling pathway. Western blotting (WB) results revealed that RPAE downregulated the protein levels of IFN-γ, p-JAK1, p-STAT1, and NF-κB in both DSS-induced UC mice and inflammation cellular model. CONCLUSIONS: RPAE alleviates DSS-induced colitis in association with suppression of the IFN-γ/JAK1/STAT1 signaling pathway. This discovery provides a potential therapeutic target for UC.

title: Mechanistic insights into the therapeutic effects of Mongolian medicine Eligengurigumu-7 against non-alcoholic fatty liver disease via the PPAR signalling pathway
abstract: BACKGROUND: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)， is characterised by a complex, multi-stage pathogenesis and progression and imposes a substantial economic burden on global public health. Thus, an urgent need exists to improve the understanding of NAFLD-related hepatic disease progression and identify effective therapeutic strategies. Eligengurigumu-7 (GRGM-7) is a common treatment prescription for liver diseases in Mongolian medicine. However, its pharmacodynamics and mechanism of action remain largely unclear. PURPOSE: To evaluate the hepatoprotective efficacy of GRGM-7 against NAFLD, identify its bioactive constituents absorbed into the bloodstream, and elucidate its key molecular targets and underlying regulatory pathways. METHODS: The key differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and pathways during the progression of NAFLD-related hepatic diseases were identified through bioinformatics analysis and immunofluorescence validation of clinical samples. NAFLD mouse models induced with either a high-fat diet (HFD) or a methionine- and choline-deficient diet (MCD) were established. The therapeutic effects of GRGM-7 against NAFLD were evaluated in these models by comparing the physiological, biochemical, and pathological indicators of the control groups, model groups, and each dose treatment group. Through RNA-sequencing and non-targeted metabolomics analysis and the combined analysis of multi-source datasets, the key pharmacodynamic targets, regulatory function directions, and regulatory pathways of GRGM-7 involved in improving NAFLD were identified and verified through reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) and western blotting (WB) experiments. The chemical components of GRGM-7 were identified using ultra performance liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS), and the compounds absorbed into the bloodstream (CABs) were identified and analysed based on the principles of serum pharmacochemistry. CABs were quantitatively analysed in the original herbal formulation through high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), and molecular docking was used to analyse the interaction between the CABs and active targets. The hepatoprotective effects of CABs and GRGM-7, as well as their effects on the targets were confirmed in an in vitro NAFLD model of oleic acid-induced AML-12 cells. Additionally, PPARγ and ACLY were subjected to siRNA-mediated silencing, and fenofibrate was used as a pharmacological agonist of PPARα to further functionally validate the involvement of the PPAR signaling pathway and ACLY in the effects of GRGM-7. RESULTS: Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) signalling was a crucial pathway involved in NAFLD-related hepatic disease progression. GRGM-7 administration ameliorated MCD- and HFD-induced NAFLD in mice and protected the liver by regulating the PPAR signalling pathway, promoting fatty acid metabolism, and maintaining liver lipid homeostasis. ATP citrate lyase (ACLY) served as a key candidate target associated with the progression of NAFLD and therapeutic action of GRGM-7. GRGM-7 contained several chemical components that were absorbed into the bloodstream. Among these CABs, cosmosiin exhibited a high affinity for key DEGs and crucial targets within signalling pathways. Moreover, cosmosiin showed a favourable hepatoprotective effect on the NAFLD cell model induced in vitro. GRGM-7 exhibited the strongest hepatoprotective effect in vitro, accompanied by modulation of the PPAR signalling pathway. Silencing of ACLY or PPARγ alleviated metabolic abnormalities, whereas subsequent GRGM-7 treatment produced further improvements. Fenofibrate treatment similarly ameliorated the OA-induced metabolic abnormalities, whereas combined treatment with fenofibrate and GRGM-7 further enhanced these effects, supporting the involvement of the PPAR signalling pathway and ACLY in the metabolic effects of GRGM-7. CONCLUSION: PPAR signalling was the key pathway involved in the progression of NAFLD-related hepatic diseases, and ACLY was one of the key potential targets. GRGM-7 regulated the PPAR signalling pathway by modulating fatty acid metabolism, thereby exerting a hepatoprotective effect. These findings highlight the potential utility of GRGM-7 as a therapeutic agent for NAFLD.

title: Astragaloside IV–loaded exosomes embedded in a GelMA hydrogel enhance angiogenesis and macrophage polarization to accelerate diabetic wound healing
abstract: Background Diabetic wound healing is severely compromised by prolonged inflammation, poor neovascularization, and defective extracellular matrix remodeling. Astragaloside IV (AS-IV), a major bioactive component of Astragalus mongholicus, has shown anti-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic activities that may benefit wound repair. However, its poor water solubility and limited local retention restrict its therapeutic efficacy. Methods Exosomes derived from human umbilical vein endothelial cells (Exo HUVECs ) were loaded with AS-IV to generate AS-IV@Exo HUVECs and then embedded in a gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) hydrogel to form AS-IV@Exo HUVECs @GelMA (AEG). The effects of this formulation on endothelial migration, tube formation, and macrophage polarization were evaluated in vitro. A streptozotocin-induced diabetic wound model was used to assess local retention, wound closure, angiogenesis, inflammation, and tissue remodeling in vivo. Finally, transcriptomic and validation analyses were performed to explore potential molecular mechanisms. Results AS-IV@Exo HUVECs promoted endothelial cell migration and tube formation, while driving macrophage polarization toward a pro-repair phenotype under inflammatory conditions. In the diabetic wound model, AEG prolonged local retention and sustained bioactivity at the wound site. Moreover, AEG treatment accelerated wound closure, improved perfusion, enhanced re-epithelialization, and promoted collagen remodeling. These effects were accompanied by increased CD31 and VEGFA expression, reduced CD86, increased CD206, decreased IL-6, and increased IL-10 in wound tissues. RNA-seq identified differences in inflammatory recruitment and cellular stress pathways between AEG- and EG-treated wounds, and subsequent validation showed changes in p53, p21, cleaved caspase-3, and Notch-related markers. Conclusion Overall, AEG hydrogel promoted diabetic wound healing, at least in part by enhancing angiogenesis and reparative macrophage polarization. This formulation may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for diabetic wounds.

title: Imperatorin exerts anti-colorectal cancer effects by targeting NOX2 to inhibit mast cell degranulation
abstract: Background Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a major global malignancy with a poor prognosis in advanced stages. Aberrant mast cell activation within the tumor microenvironment (TME) drives CRC progression; however, the molecular mechanisms underlying the tumor-promoting role of mast cells in the hypoxic TME remain unclear, and effective therapies targeting these cells are lacking. Objective To investigate the role of the NADPH oxidase 2 (NOX2)-reactive oxygen species (ROS)-calcium signaling axis in mast cell activation and evaluate the anti-CRC activity of imperatorin (IMP), a natural furanocoumarin. Methods Human mast cell and CRC cell lines were used to establish hypoxic activation and conditioned medium co-culture systems. Tissue microarrays, single‑cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets and CT26 allograft mouse models were employed, combined with gain/loss-of-function, Western Blot, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), immunofluorescence and cell functional assays. Results NOX2 expression was significantly upregulated in activated mast cells from human CRC tissues. IMP inhibited NOX2, thereby blocking hypoxia-induced oxidative stress and mast cell degranulation. This intervention suppressed the secretion of tumor-promoting mediators and effectively inhibited CRC cell proliferation and invasion. Furthermore, in vivo experiments demonstrated that IMP dose-dependently suppressed CRC allograft growth in murine models without causing overt systemic toxicity. Conclusion This study reveals a mechanism by which mast cells promote CRC progression in the hypoxic TME and demonstrates that IMP exerts potent anti-CRC effects by targeting NOX2 to inhibit mast cell activation. These findings identify both a therapeutic target and a promising lead compound for TME-targeted CRC therapy.

title: Aspirin eugenol ester attenuates alcoholic liver injury via the NRF2/SLC7A11/GPX4 pathway-mediated ferroptosis suppression
abstract: Background Alcoholic liver injury (ALI) is a prevalent chronic liver disease worldwide and represents a major public health burden. Previous pharmacological and pharmacodynamic studies have indicated that aspirin eugenol ester (AEE) exerts multiple pharmacological activities, including protective effects against non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. However, whether AEE can ameliorate ALI and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Purpose This study sought to explore the protective effects of AEE on ALI and to delineate the associated molecular mechanisms. Methods This study investigated the protective effects of AEE against ALI using both in vitro and in vivo models, with a particular focus on elucidating its molecular mechanisms. Results In cellular models, AEE significantly alleviated ethanol- and erastin-induced cytotoxicity and morphological damage, while markedly reversing abnormalities in superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity, malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, Fe 2+ accumulation, reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, 4-Hydroxynonenal levels and lipid peroxidation. Mechanistically, AEE attenuated ethanol-induced ferroptosis by activating the NRF2/SLC7A11/GPX4 antioxidant axis. This result was validated in primary mouse hepatocytes. In animal models, AEE markedly improved alcohol-induced metabolic disturbances, including dyslipidemia, glucose disorders, and hepatic steatosis, while restoring hepatic redox homeostasis and ethanol metabolism through upregulation of alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) and aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) and suppression of CYP2E1. Consistently, AEE enhanced NRF2 signaling and ferroptosis resistance in liver tissues, as evidenced by increased expression of SLC7A11, GPX4, ferritin, and HO-1, along with reduced expression of BAP1, Keap1 and P53. Conclusions AEE exerts a potent protective effect against ALI by attenuating ethanol-induced ferroptosis via activation of the NRF2/SLC7A11/GPX4 signaling pathway, thereby improving hepatic metabolic homeostasis.

title: Polypharmacological targeting of atopic dermatitis by natural products: A mechanism-driven systematic review
abstract: Background Atopic dermatitis (AD) involves interconnected disturbances in epidermal barrier function, immune regulation, microbial homeostasis, and neuroimmune itch. Natural products influence several of these processes, but their mechanistic and clinical evidence remains fragmented. Purpose To assess natural product-based interventions for AD within a polypharmacological framework and identify priorities for clinical translation. Study design Mechanism-driven systematic review with qualitative narrative synthesis. Methods PubMed and the Web of Science Core Collection were searched from inception to March 2026. Eligible studies evaluated isolated natural compounds, characterized extracts or formulations, natural lipids, or microbe-derived interventions in patients with AD or validated experimental models. Evidence was synthesized by chemotype, pathological axis, molecular target or pathway, study design, and translational relevance. Results A total of 156 original studies were retained. Reported effects clustered around epidermal differentiation and lipid homeostasis, inflammatory signaling, host-microbial interactions, and pruriceptive pathways. Preclinical studies provided mechanistic evidence for barrier-restorative, immunomodulatory, microbiome-related, and antipruritic effects involving multiple pathways. Clinical studies reported improvements in disease severity, barrier-related measures, pruritus, and quality of life, although findings varied across interventions and study designs. Direct target engagement, exposure-response relationships, and contributions of individual constituents in multicomponent preparations remained incompletely resolved. Conclusion Natural products provide a pharmacologically diverse basis for intervention across interconnected AD pathways. Current evidence supports therapeutic potential and multitarget activity, although polypharmacological synergy, comparative efficacy, and long-term safety require further validation. Clinical translation requires reproducible product characterization, direct mechanistic validation, pharmacokinetic assessment, human-relevant models, and well-designed clinical studies.

title: Modulating pMMR colorectal tumors toward a dMMR-like phenotype by Xian-Lian-Jie-Du decoction enhances anti-PD-1 efficacy
abstract: Background In advanced colorectal cancer (CRC), only approximately 5% of patients harbor deficient DNA mismatch repair (dMMR) tumors, which are responsive to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), whereas the remaining 95% with proficient mismatch repair (pMMR) derive limited benefit. Purpose To investigate whether the Chinese medicinal formulation Xian-Lian-Jie-Du decoction (XLJDD) can modulate pMMR colorectal tumors toward a dMMR-like phenotype, thereby enhancing their responsiveness to anti-PD-1 therapy. Study design We employed an integrative approach using isogenic pMMR/dMMR mouse models, combining in vivo efficacy assessment, mechanistic dissection, and bioactive compound screening to elucidate how XLJDD overcomes immunotherapy resistance. Methods We developed a pMMR/dMMR mouse model to assess the efficacy of XLJDD in conjunction with anti-PD-1 therapy. The therapeutic outcomes were examined using histopathological evaluation, immunofluorescence, and flow cytometry analyses. The mechanisms underlying XLJDD's effects were elucidated through transcriptomic, proteomic, and single-cell transcriptomic approaches. Additionally, ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) was employed to analyze the constituents of XLJDD. Results We demonstrate that XLJDD sensitizes pMMR tumors to anti-PD-1 treatment, achieving efficacy comparable to that observed in dMMR tumors. Mechanistically, we reveal that pMMR tumor cells evade immune killing by downregulating and concealing interferon-gamma receptor 1 (IFNGR1) from the cell surface, thereby weakening interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) signaling. XLJDD overcomes this immune evasion by restoring IFNGR1 abundance and membrane localization, which amplifies IFN-γ-JAK2-STAT1 signaling and augments cytotoxic immune responses. We further identify Bilobalide A, an active component of XLJDD, as a critical factor in stabilizing IFNGR1 at the membrane and enhancing immunotherapeutic sensitivity in pMMR tumors. Conclusion These findings establish IFNGR1 expression and membrane localization as critical determinants of IFN-γ mediated tumor cell killing and identify XLJDD and its active component Bilobalide A as pharmacological strategies to target this pathway, providing a rationale for expanding the clinical benefit of anti-PD-1 therapy in pMMR CRC patients.

title: Oudemansiella raphanipes polysaccharide alleviates DSS-induced colitis associated with gut microbiota and ZBP1-associated PANoptosis
abstract: Background Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic relapsing inflammatory bowel disease with limited preventive options. The edible mushroom Oudemansiella raphanipes produces polysaccharides with reported bioactivity, but the effects of its purified fraction Oudemansiella raphanipes polysaccharide (UAE-ORP) on colitis remain unknown. Purpose and methods UAE-ORP was evaluated in mice with sodium dextran sulphate (DSS)-induced colitis using metagenomic and metabolomic analysis, as well as histological, ELISA and Western blot analysis of intestinal barrier function, ZBP1-associated PANoptosis-related proteins, and FFAR2/FFAR3 expression. Results UAE-ORP alleviated DSS-induced colonic injury, reducing the DAI scores to 1.7 ± 0.3-2.7 ± 0.5 across treatment groups and restoring colon length to 6.2 ± 0.9-8.2 ± 0.8 cm across doses. UAE-ORP was associated with attenuated ZBP1-associated PANoptosis-related protein expression, increased Lachnospiraceae abundance, and restored acetic acid and 3,4-dihydroxyphthalate levels. UAE-ORP also restored the protein expression levels of FFAR2 and FFAR3. Correlation analysis suggested a potential association between Lachnospiraceae-related metabolites and FFAR2/FFAR3 signaling. Conclusion UAE-ORP alleviates DSS-induced colitis in mice. The protective effects coincide with altered gut microbiota composition, elevated microbial metabolites, restored FFAR2/FFAR3 expression, and concomitant changes in ZBP1-associated PANoptosis-related protein. These observations identify several candidate pathways warranting further investigation and provide preliminary mechanistic context for the anti-colitic activity of this mushroom polysaccharide.

title: Berberine increases the sensitivity of sorafenib in human hepatocellular carcinoma via inducing HIF-1α-mediated energy crisis
abstract: Background Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) often develops resistance to sorafenib (SORA), a multikinase inhibitor that has long been a cornerstone of systemic therapy for advanced HCC, leading to cancer progression and poor survival. Strategies to enhance the therapeutic efficacy of SORA in HCC are therefore urgently needed. Purpose This study aimed to investigate whether berberine (BBR), a natural isoquinoline alkaloid, could act as a metabolic modulator to overcome SORA resistance in HCC and to elucidate the underlying metabolic mechanisms. Methods In vitro and in vivo models, transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses, genetic rescue experiments, and clinical tissue microarray analysis were employed to evaluate the sensitizing effect of BBR in SORA-resistant HCC. Results BBR enhanced the antitumor efficacy of SORA to suppress HCC cell proliferation, induce apoptosis, and reduce orthotopic tumor growth in mice. Transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses revealed that BBR disrupted energy homeostasis by concurrently inhibiting glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation. Mechanistically, BBR suppressed hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α), thereby downregulating the key glucose-metabolizing enzymes phosphofructokinase platelet type (PFKP) and lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) in HCC cells. Restoration of PFKP and LDHA expression or stabilization of HIF-1α reversed the metabolic and antitumor effects of BBR and SORA cotreatment. Clinically, HIF-1α, PFKP, and LDHA were overexpressed in HCC tissues and correlated with molecular features previously linked to SORA resistance. Conclusion These findings provide functional evidence that BBR sensitizes HCC to SORA by inducing an HIF-1α/PFKP/LDHA-mediated energy crisis, highlighting the preclinical potential of BBR as a candidate adjuvant agent for overcoming SORA resistance in HCC.

title: Zuojin Wan reverses cetuximab resistance in KRAS-mutant colorectal cancer via the NRF2-GCH1/CoQ and DHODH/CoQ axes
abstract: Background Cetuximab (CET), a monoclonal antibody targeting the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), serves as a cornerstone therapeutic option for advanced colorectal cancer (CRC). However, patients with KRAS-mutant CRC present inherent resistance to CET, which directly compromises its clinical efficacy and therapeutic benefits. Zuojin Wan (ZJW), a classic traditional Chinese medicine formula consisting of Coptis chinensis Franch. and Evodia rutaecarpa (Juss.) Benth., has been documented to exert potent antitumor activity; nevertheless, its potential role in reversing CET resistance in KRAS-mutated CRC and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly defined. Purpose This study aimed to investigate the efficacy of ZJW in overcoming CET resistance in KRAS-mutated CRC and further characterize its key molecular targets and regulatory mechanisms. Methods In vitro experiments were conducted using two KRAS-mutated CRC cell lines, HCT116 and SW620. The synergistic antiproliferative effect of ZJW combined with CET was assessed via CCK-8 assay and colony formation assay. Ferroptosis induction mediated by the combination treatment was verified by measuring lipid peroxidation, glutathione (GSH) depletion, ferrous ion (Fe2+) accumulation, and observing characteristic mitochondrial morphological alterations using transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels were detected to evaluate intracellular oxidative stress. Transcriptome sequencing, Western blot analysis and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) were performed to explore the underlying molecular mechanisms, while plasmid transfection and quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) were carried out for functional validation. A nude mouse subcutaneous xenograft model was established to evaluate the antitumor efficacy of the combined treatment in vivo, and immunohistochemical (IHC) staining was performed to detect the expression of relevant proteins. The primary bioactive components of ZJW were identified by mass spectrometry, and network pharmacology analysis was performed to predict the potential interactions between these active components and CRC-related signaling pathways. Results ZJW synergistically augmented the CET-mediated suppression of KRAS-mutated CRC cell proliferation and triggered significant ferroptosis, as evidenced by elevated lipid peroxidation, reduced GSH levels, increased Fe2+ accumulation, shrunken mitochondria with condensed cristae, and markedly enhanced intracellular oxidative stress. Combination treatment with ZJW and CET significantly downregulated the expression of core proteins involved in the parallel NRF2-GCH1/CoQ and DHODH/CoQ antioxidant axes, thereby disrupting intracellular redox homeostasis. Silencing of NRF2 or DHODH facilitated ferroptosis and sensitized CRC cells to CET, whereas overexpression of these two molecules abolished the synergistic antitumor effect of ZJW plus CET. In the nude mouse xenograft model, the combined regimen notably suppressed tumor growth and decreased tumor weight, and modulated the expression of ferroptosis-associated markers (NRF2, DHODH) and the lipid peroxidation indicator 4-HNE in tumor tissues. Mass spectrometry identified the major bioactive constituents of ZJW, and network pharmacology analysis predicted their potential involvement in multiple CRC-related pathways, including antioxidant defense and ferroptosis regulation. Conclusion ZJW reverses CET resistance in KRAS-mutated CRC by inhibiting the parallel NRF2-GCH1/CoQ and DHODH/CoQ antioxidant axes to induce ferroptosis. This study provides a solid scientific basis for the clinical translation of ZJW as an adjuvant therapeutic strategy to boost the efficacy of CET in CRC treatment.

title: Artemisitene targets GLIS3 to inhibit the NF-κB-TNF signaling pathway and suppress bladder cancer cell growth
abstract: BACKGROUND: Artemisia annua, a medicinal and edible herb best known for Artemisinin, exhibits broad pharmacological activities and considerable clinical value. However, its therapeutic potential in bladder cancer remains largely unexplored. PURPOSE: Here, we systematically investigated the anti-bladder cancer efficacy of Artemisitene (ATT) in vitro and in vivo and delineated its underlying mechanisms. METHODS: Using cell-based and animal models, we found that ATT robustly suppressed bladder cancer cell growth. Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic sequencing, combined with MST assays and transient transfection, revealed the mechanism of ATT inhibiting the progression of bladder cancer. In addition, we analysed single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets and performed virtual knockout experiments to investigate the expression pattern and potential functional role of the ATT target gene GLIS3 across different pathological stages of bladder cancer. RESULTS: GLIS3 expression was higher in tumour than in adjacent nontumor tissues in BLCA patients and was further elevated in intermediate/late stages (T3-T4) compared with early stages (T1-T2). Consistently, single-cell RNA-seq data showed that GLIS3 levels in epithelial cells were higher in T3-T4 than in T1-T2 BLCA. Moreover, in virtual GLIS3 knockout in BLCA epithelial cells negatively regulated TNF and NF-κB signalling pathways. ATT directly interacts with GLIS3 and destabilizes the protein, consequently suppressing the transcription of NF-κB and TNF. Mutation of GLIS3 at Arg-404 and Pro-411 markedly weakened its interaction with ATT and partly abrogated the pharmacological effects of ATT. Moreover, GLIS3 knockdown enhanced the inhibitory effect of Gem on bladder cancer cells, while ATT further potentiated Gem-mediated suppression of BLCA by downregulating GLIS3 expression. CONCLUSIONS: ATT binds to GLIS3 and decreases its protein stability, thereby suppressing the transcription of NF-κB and TNF, inducing apoptosis in bladder cancer cells, and inhibiting cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. These findings provide a mechanistic rationale for developing ATT as a potential therapeutic agent or dietary supplement for bladder cancer and expand the medicinal value of Artemisia annua derivatives.

title: Cinnamaldehyde protects against early diabetic retinopathy: an integrative In vivo and computational study
abstract: Background Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a leading cause of vision impairment, and current treatments are limited to advanced stages. Cinnamaldehyde (CA), the primary bioactive constituent of cinnamon, has demonstrated anti-apoptotic and anti-diabetic properties, but its role and mechanism in early DR remain unexplored. This study investigated whether CA protects against early DR and whether the effect is associated with phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT) pathway activation. Purpose This study investigated whether CA exerts anti‑apoptotic effects in early DR and whether these effects are associated with PI3K/AKT pathway phosphorylation. Network pharmacology, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and ADMET prediction were employed as hypothesis‑generating and supportive computational tools to predict potential key targets, validate binding stability, and assess drug‑likeness. Methods Diabetes was induced in rats by streptozotocin. After 8 weeks of hyperglycemia, diabetic rats received daily oral CA (100 mg/kg) or vehicle until week 20. Retinal morphology and apoptosis were assessed by H&E and TUNEL staining. Expression of PI3K/AKT pathway components and apoptosis‑related markers was analyzed by immunohistochemistry, RT‑qPCR and Western blot. Network pharmacology was used to predict CA targets and DR‑related genes, followed by GO and KEGG enrichment. Molecular docking was performed on 10 targets (Bcl‑2, Bax, XIAP, CASP3, IL6, ERBB2, TNF‑α, EGFR, BDNF, AKT2), with subsequent 100‑ns molecular dynamics simulations and MM‑GBSA binding free energy calculations for four key targets (ERBB2, AKT2, Bcl‑2, TNF‑α). ADMET properties were predicted using ADMETlab 3.0. Results CA did not lower blood glucose or prevent weight loss in diabetic rats (p > 0.05 vs. diabetic controls). However, CA was associated with ameliorated retinal histological changes and a reduction in TUNEL-positive cells in the ganglion cell layer (from 37.33 ± 7.09% to 18.67 ± 2.25%, p Conclusion CA treatment was associated with amelioration of retinal histological changes and a reduction in TUNEL-positive cells in the GCL under persistent hyperglycemia, without a detected improvement in fasting glucose. The observed changes were associated with PI3K/AKT phosphorylation and modulation of apoptotic regulators. Computational analyses provide exploratory, hypothesis-generating evidence. The correlational nature of the PI3K/AKT findings, the absence of causal pathway intervention, and the exploratory nature of the computational predictions should be considered when interpreting these results.

title: Kaempferide promotes melanogenesis through miR-145-associated glutathione depletion with partial ROS contribution
abstract: Background Despite the pathological link between vitiligo and both oxidative stress and melanin dysregulation, reactive oxygen species (ROS)-modulating therapies show limited efficacy. Kaempferide, a compound from Vernonia anthelmintica (L.) Willd, promotes glutathione (GSH)-dependent melanogenesis, yet its mechanism of action in vitiligo treatment remains to be fully elucidated. Purpose This study aimed to elucidate whether kaempferide-induced melanogenesis is associated with GSH depletion and the underlying regulatory mechanism. Methods B16F10 cells, primary melanocytes from C57BL/6 J mice, and zebrafish larval models were used to investigate the role of GSH/thiol homeostasis in kaempferide-induced melanogenesis using biochemical, fluorescence-based, transcriptomic, miR-145-5p mimic transfection, and connectivity-mapping approaches. Results Kaempferide increased melanogenesis in cells and zebrafish and reduced intracellular thiol/GSH levels, accompanied by an increase in ROS. Further, it also reduced the expression of GSH-metabolic genes and proteins. NAC attenuated, whereas BSO potentiated, kaempferide-induced melanogenic responses, supporting GSH depletion as a major biochemical event. Transcriptomic analysis showed decreased miR-145 and increased Mest expression, and miR-145-5p mimic attenuated both kaempferide-induced melanogenesis and the accompanying reduction in thiol/GSH levels. CMap analysis further provided hypothesis-generating associations between kaempferide-responsive signatures and miR-145-associated regulatory networks. Conclusions Kaempferide-induced melanogenesis is a GSH-dependent process with miR-145-associated regulation whereas ROS contributes partially and appears to act in a secondary manner.

title: Natural products as modulators of cuproptosis: A systematic review of mechanisms, therapeutic potential, and future directions
abstract: Background Cuproptosis is a copper ion-dependent form of regulated cell death discovered in 2022. Its mechanism lies in the binding of copper to acylated proteins in the tricarboxylic acid cycle, thereby triggering proteotoxic stress. Natural products, with their structural diversity and good biocompatibility, are gradually becoming regulators of cuproptosis. Purpose To systematically clarify the mechanisms by which natural products regulate cuproptosis, identify its core targets, and evaluate its therapeutic potential, with a particular focus on cancer therapy and neurodegenerative diseases. Methods Literature from PubMed and CNKI up to August 1, 2026 was retrieved using keywords including "cuproptosis", "copper ionophore", and "natural product", etc.; studies on natural product intervention in cuproptosis in tumors, neurodegenerative diseases, and cardiovascular diseases were screened and included, and the molecular mechanisms, regulatory modes, and therapeutic prospects were comprehensively analyzed. Results The core cuproptosis axis involves FDX1-mediated reduction of Cu 2+ to Cu + , binding of Cu + to lipoylated DLAT, and mitochondrial dysfunction. This axis is tightly controlled by copper homeostasis proteins (SLC31A1, ATP7A/B). Natural products bifunctionally modulate cuproptosis. Specifically, they induce tumor cell cuproptosis by elevating intracellular copper or disrupting copper metabolism, and protect normal cells via copper chelation or FDX1 inhibition. Such strategies benefit tumor drug resistance reversal and neuroprotection in neurodegenerative diseases, but their development is restricted by unclear mechanisms, poor druggability and insufficient clinical translation. Conclusion Natural products are versatile modulators of cuproptosis with dual utility as probes and lead compounds. Future work should identify direct targets, improve druggability, and enable clinical translation.

title: Xanthatin overcomes osimertinib resistance by disturbing cholesterol metabolism via targeting HMGCR protein degradation in NSCLC
abstract: Background Osimertinib is a third-generation, irreversible EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), nevertheless, the inevitable occurrence of osimertinib resistance after a long-term administration limits its clinical application in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Xanthatin, a naturally active component from Xanthium Strumarium L., has been shown to possess multiple bioactive effects. However, whether xanthatin can ameliorate osimertinib resistance remains unclear. Purpose The present study aimed to clarify the role and detailed mechanism of xanthatin in reversing osimertinib resistance in NSCLC. Methods Combenefit analysis, LDH release assay, and EdU staining were employed to evaluate the effect of xanthatin on osimertinib cytotoxicity in osimertinib-resistant (OR) NSCLC cells. Quantitative proteomics combined with bioinformatics and network pharmacology analysis was used to uncover the specific target of xanthatin. Xanthatin-triggered HMGCR protein degradation was assessed by bio-layer interferometry, drug affinity responsive target stability assay, cycloheximide chase assay and ubiquitination determination. The function of xanthatin on cholesterol homeostasis was measured via the detection of HMGCR activity, total cholesterol, triglycerides and lipid droplets as well as MDR1 distribution in the lipid rafts. The function of MDR1 was examined via a rhodamine 123 efflux assay. The accumulation and efflux of osimertinib were monitored using FITC-labeled osimertinib. The effect of HMGCR on the cytotoxicity of xanthatin was evaluated through a series of in vitro and in vivo experiments in HMGCR-overexpressing NSCLC OR cells. Results Xanthatin restored the sensitivity of NSCLC OR cells to osimertinib, accompanied by the induction of oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Proteomic data indicate that oxidative stress and metabolic reprogramming contribute to xanthatin-induced apoptosis in NSCLC OR cells. Through further integration with network pharmacology, we identified HMGCR (a key enzyme of cholesterol metabolism) as a potential target of xanthatin. We confirmed xanthatin directly binds to HMGCR protein (K D =6.753 μM), subsequently facilitating AMFR-mediated K48-linked ubiquitination and degradation of HMGCR. Xanthatin diminished intracellular cholesterol biosynthesis and MDR1 levels in lipid rafts. HMGCR overexpression mitigated the cytotoxicity of xanthatin and sustained cholesterol homeostasis, enabling tolerance to the combined effects of xanthatin and osimertinib. Conversely, HMGCR-deficient NSCLC OR cells were more vulnerable to osimertinib. Conclusion Our study demonstrates for the first time that xanthatin directly binds to HMGCR and promotes AMFR-mediated K48-linked ubiquitination of HMGCR, which in turn accelerates HMGCR degradation through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, leading to reduced cholesterol synthesis, less distribution of MDR1 in lipid rafts, ROS accumulation, and mitochondrial dysfunction-associated apoptosis, ultimately restoring osimertinib sensitivity in NSCLC cells. Therefore, xanthatin may represent a preclinical natural product candidate for the reversal of osimertinib resistance in NSCLC cells, which requires further translational verification in future studies.

title: Schistosomicidal potential of usnic acid: In vivo and in silico insights
authors: Ana Maria Mendonça de Albuquerque Melo
Mônica Camelo Pessoa de Azevedo Albuquerque

title: Ginkgolide B drives cardiomyocyte proliferation and myocardial regeneration through TLR4/NF-κB/HIF-1α-regulated glycolytic reprogramming
abstract: Background Myocardial infarction (MI) continues to contribute substantially to global mortality and is characterized by irreversible cardiomyocyte loss and limited regenerative capacity in the adult heart. Ginkgolide B (GB), a bioactive compound used in traditional Chinese medicine, has well-documented cardioprotective effects; however, whether it promotes cardiomyocyte proliferation and myocardial regeneration, and through which mechanisms, remains unclear. Purpose This study aimed to investigate the therapeutic potential and underlying molecular mechanisms of GB in promoting cardiomyocyte proliferation and cardiac regeneration. Methods The therapeutic effects of GB were assessed in cardiomyocyte (CM) cell lines and mouse models of apical resection (AR) and MI. To define the underlying mechanism, we combined network pharmacology, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, RNA sequencing, and targeted metabolite profiling. The interaction between GB and TLR4 was evaluated using a cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA). The dependency on the TLR4/NF-κB/HIF-1α pathway and glycolysis were pharmacologically validated using 2-deoxy-d-glucose (2-DG, glycolysis inhibitor) and Bay 11-7082 (NF-κB inhibitor). Results GB enhanced CM proliferation and angiogenesis in vitro, and improved cardiac function, reduced infarct size, and promoted CM proliferation in neonatal and adult mouse models. Mechanistically, GB interacted directly with TLR4, activated the NF-κB/HIF-1α signaling axis, and promoted a shift toward glycolytic metabolism. Inhibition of NF-κB or glycolysis abolished GB-induced CM proliferation, glycolytic activity, and myocardial regeneration. Conclusions GB promotes cardiomyocyte proliferation and cardiac regeneration through TLR4/NF-κB/HIF-1α-dependent regulation of glycolytic metabolism. These findings support the potential of GB as a plant-derived therapeutic candidate for ischemic heart disease.

title: Corrigendum to “Total glucosides of paeony modulates leucine metabolism by inhibiting SLC7A5, antagonizing mTOR signaling to suppress head and neck squamous cell carcinoma” [Phytomedicine 159 (2026) 158576]
Corrigendum to “Targeting USP4 to inhibit TGF-β signaling: the antifibrotic potential of isovitexin in renal interstitial fibrosis” [Phytomedicine 155 (2026) 158141]
Bushen Huoxue Formula promotes osteoporotic fracture healing by CGRP-mediated dual regulation of BMSCs-osteoclasts balance through modulating mitochondrial energy metabolism
abstract: Osteoporotic fracture (OPF) is a serious complication that severely impairs the quality of life. Bushen Huoxue Formula (BHF), a clinically established prescription based on the TCM principle of "tonifying the kidney and activating blood circulation," has been widely used to treat osteoporosis. However, its efficacy in OPF and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, using a rat OPF model, we found that BHF treatment significantly accelerated the fracture healing process and improved callus microstructure and mineralization. Multi-omics analysis revealed that its therapeutic effect was closely associated with the regulation of mitochondrial energy metabolism, identifying CGRP as a key differential target. Mechanistically, CGRP was upregulated in bone mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs), where it enhanced mitochondrial energy metabolism and promoted osteogenic differentiation. Conversely, in osteoclast precursor RAW264.7 cells, CGRP was downregulated and inhibited osteoclast differentiation, demonstrating its dual regulatory role in bone remodeling via the same target. Further studies showed that taurine, a major component of BHF, could recapitulate the formula's effects by modulating CGRP to promote osteogenesis and suppress osteoclastogenesis. Importantly, corroborative clinical research demonstrated that BHF treatment effectively alleviated clinical symptoms and promoted fracture repair in OPF patients. In summary, BHF facilitates OPF healing through CGRP mediated mitochondrial energy metabolism, providing both mechanistic insight and clinical evidence for its repositioning from osteoporosis to fracture management.

title: Antitumor potential of medicinal plants from the Brazilian Cerrado: a systematic review of experimental studies
abstract: BACKGROUND: The Brazilian Cerrado harbors 12,180 cataloged angiosperm species; 7395 (60.7%) are endemic to Brazil, and its flora has been used in traditional medicine for generations. Regardless, the antitumor potential of these species has been investigated in a fragmented manner. PURPOSE: To compile and analyze experimental evidence on the antitumor effects of preparations derived from Cerrado plant species in vitro and in vivo models. METHODS: Searches were conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Scopus, without date restrictions and limited to publications in English. The methodological quality of included studies was assessed using an adapted risk-of-bias assessment tool. RESULTS: Sixty-two studies were included; 55 employed in vitro models and 12 employed in vivo models, five of which combined both approaches. The studies encompassed a broad range of malignancies, including melanoma, leukemias, glioblastoma, and breast, prostate, and colorectal cancers, and evaluated crude extracts, fractions, and isolated compounds from >40 species. The most frequently documented antitumor effects were cell viability reduction, apoptosis induction via the intrinsic mitochondrial pathway, cell cycle arrest, and matrix metalloproteinase inhibition. Annona crassiflora, Campomanesia adamantium, Stryphnodendron adstringens, and Tapirira guianensis were each reported in three or more independent studies (most frequently investigated species). Relevant methodological limitations, including a widespread absence of tumor selectivity data, pharmacokinetic profiles, and experimental blinding, were revealed. No clinical trials evaluating Cerrado plant species as oncological interventions were identified. CONCLUSION: The Cerrado flora represents a relevant source of compounds with preclinical antitumor activity, but essential translational data remain absent. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: PROSPERO database (CRD420261372222). Available from https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261372222.

title: Therapeutic efficacy and dosing regimen evidence synthesis of Ursolic Acid for liver injury: A preclinical systematic review with machine learning
abstract: Background Ursolic acid (UA), a pentacyclic triterpene, shows hepatoprotective efficacy and favorable safety in various animal models of liver injury. However, robust preclinical evidence remains scarce. Purpose To synthesize the preclinical evidence for UA and explore how UA dose and treatment duration are associated with alanine aminotransferase (ALT) improvement in animal models of liver injury. Study design This preclinical systematic review integrating meta-analysis and machine learning followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA). Methods Relevant preclinical studies through April 11, 2026 were systematically retrieved from PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, OVID, CNKI and Wanfang. Machine learning analyses were used to identify factors associated with ALT improvement, particularly human equivalent dose (HED) and treatment duration. Results Forty-seven articles were included in this analysis. UA markedly improved histopathological parameters, liver function, biochemical parameters, serum lipid levels, oxidative stress indicators, and inflammatory markers in liver injury animal models. Random forest was selected as the final predictive model. The analysis further identified model administration route, treatment duration, HED, and time of administration as key determinants for the improvement rate of ALT. An exploratory HED range of approximately 5-7 mg/kg was associated with greater predicted ALT improvement. Conclusion The study indicates that UA exerts hepatoprotective effects in animal models of liver injury. Potential mechanisms include modulation of the gut-liver axis, attenuation of hepatic and systemic oxidative stress, and suppression of inflammation and fibrosis. Given the exploratory nature of these preclinical findings, the translational potential of UA warrants further rigorous validation.

title: Identification of the Therapeutic Effects and Potential Bioactive Compounds of Shenrong Qiwei Particles in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis via Multiple Disease Models
abstract: Background Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease characterized by progressive motor neuron degeneration, leading to muscle weakness, atrophy, fasciculations, stiffness or flaccidity, and impaired speech. Traditional Chinese Medicine associates these symptoms with deficiencies in vitality and muscle support. Shenrong Qiwei (SRQW), a formula mainly composed of Ginseng and Cistanche deserticola, has shown clinical potential for ALS, but its underlying biological mechanisms remain unclear. Purpose To evaluate the therapeutic effects of SRQW across multiple ALS models and to identify its bioactive compounds responsible for neuroprotection and neuromuscular preservation. Study Design Preclinical study combining transgenic ALS mouse models, patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) neuromuscular organoids (NMOs), and iPSC-derived induced motor neurons (iMNs). Methods SRQW was administered to SOD1 and TDP43 transgenic mice to assess motor function and neuromuscular junction (NMJ) integrity. NMOs derived from ALS patient iPSCs were treated with SRQW to evaluate muscle contraction, NMJ structure, and proteinopathy. Single-nuclei RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) was performed to assess axonal growth, synaptic activity, and ALS-related gene modulation. iMNs were used for high-throughput screening of SRQW components to identify active compounds. Results SRQW significantly improved motor performance and NMJ morphology in both SOD1 and TDP43 mice. In NMOs, SRQW enhanced muscle contraction, preserved NMJ architecture, and reduced abnormal protein accumulation. snRNA-seq indicated upregulation of genes related to axonal growth and synaptic function, along with modulation of ALS-associated genes in motor neurons. Screening in iMNs identified Ginsenoside Rg2 as the most potent bioactive component, which also ameliorated proteinopathies and restored NMJ integrity in NMOs. Conclusion SRQW exerts neuroprotective and neuromuscular benefits across multiple ALS models, with Ginsenoside Rg2 emerging as a key active compound. These findings provide mechanistic insights into the multi-component efficacy of SRQW and support its potential for translational application in ALS therapy.

title: Anti-Inflammatory effects of Vietnamese coriander (Persicaria odorata (Lour.) Soják) extract in a rat paw edema model and modulation of pro-inflammatory mediators
abstract: Background Persicaria odorata (Lour.) Soják, or Vietnamese coriander, is an edible plant traditionally used to address flatulence and localized inflammation. However, scientific evidence supporting its anti-inflammatory effects and molecular mechanisms remains limited. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the anti-inflammatory effects of 50% ethanolic leaf extract of P. odorata (PO) in a carrageenan-induced rat paw edema model and to elucidate its possible mechanisms of action. Methods PO was phytochemically characterized by identifying selected phytochemical markers using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). Acute oral toxicity was evaluated in rats following the OECD Guideline 423. The anti-inflammatory activity was investigated using the carrageenan-induced paw edema model by assessing paw volume, histopathological changes, polymorphonuclear cell (PMN) infiltration, myeloperoxidase (MPO) activity, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and inflammation-related gene expression. In silico studies were also conducted to investigate possible interactions between selected phytochemicals and inflammation-related targets. Results HPLC analysis confirmed the presence of gallic acid, rutin, myricetin, and quercetin as selected phytochemical markers. No evident acute toxicity was observed at the tested doses. In the carrageenan-induced paw edema model, PO significantly reduced paw volume, PMN infiltration, MPO activity, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and interleukin-1β (IL-1β) levels. Furthermore, PO significantly downregulated the mRNA expression of inflammation-related genes. In silico analyses suggested nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB)- and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK)-related pathways as potential molecular targets. Conclusions PO possesses significant anti-inflammatory activity by suppressing inflammatory mediators and reducing inflammatory cell infiltration and may modulate NF-κB and MAPK-related pathways, as suggested by computational analyses.

title: A small molecule utilizes both antivirulence and host-directed mechanisms to combat bacterial infection
abstract: Background Antimicrobial resistance is progressively undermining the efficacy of conventional antibiotics, and intracellular infections caused by Salmonella typhimurium (ST) remain difficult to eradicate, underscoring the need for alternative therapeutic strategies. Purpose To identify natural small molecules possessing both antivirulence and host-directed activities against ST infection, and further characterize their mechanisms of action. Methods A dual-screening strategy was employed to identify compounds that inhibit both ST invasion and intracellular replication. RNA sequencing, quantitative polymerase chain reaction, western blot analysis, β-galactosidase reporter assay, scanning electron microscopy, and flow cytometry were performed to investigate the mode of action of the active compound. A murine enterocolitis model was established to evaluate its therapeutic efficacy. Results Ferulic acid (FA) emerged as a dual-acting inhibitor. FA suppressed SPI-4 promoter PsiiA activity, reduced SPI-4 transcription and SiiE secretion, and impaired SiiE-dependent adhesion, thereby limiting bacterial invasion. In parallel, FA suppressed macrophage STAT3 phosphorylation and enhanced NRF2 signaling, leading to reduced intracellular ferrous iron and ferroptosis, which in turn restricted intracellular bacterial replication. Furthermore, FA treatment alleviated ST-induced enterocolitis in mice. Conclusions FA protects against ST infection by attenuating bacterial virulence and modulating host iron homeostasis. These findings support its potential as a combined antivirulence and host-directed therapeutic candidate.

title: Dihydrotanshinone I suppresses ovarian cancer by targeting splicing factor SRSF1 to regulate the long non-coding RNA SLC8A1-AS1/FOXO1 axis
abstract: Background Ovarian cancer (OC) is a lethal malignancy with limited therapies. The natural compound dihydrotanshinone I (DHT) exhibits broad antitumor activity, yet its precise molecular targets and mechanistic interplay with oncogenic lncRNAs in OC remain largely unexplored. Purpose This study aimed to investigate the molecular targets and underlying mechanisms of DHT‑regulated lncRNAs in OC. Study design DHT efficacy was evaluated in vitro and in vivo. Mechanisms were investigated via lncRNA profiling, transcriptomic analysis, functional assays, and protein‑binding experiments. Methods The antitumor efficacy of DHT was assessed in OC cells and xenograft models. LncRNA candidates were screened using microarray and validated by clinical cohort analysis. The regulatory role of SLC8A1-AS1 was further verified through functional assays. RNA pull-down/MS and RIP were performed to identify proteins binding to SLC8A1-AS1. Rescue experiments were conducted to evaluate whether SRSF1 influences SLC8A1-AS1 stability. The DHT-SRSF1 interaction and binding sites were examined through SPR, CETSA, DARTS, MS, and molecular docking. Transcriptomics and western blot were conducted to analyze downstream signaling cascades. Results DHT significantly suppressed OC growth. SLC8A1-AS1 was highly expressed and associated with poor prognosis in OC. Mechanistically, SRSF1 bound to SLC8A1-AS1 and enhanced its stability, activating the PI3K/AKT/FOXO1 pathway. DHT directly bound to SRSF1 and induced its degradation, downregulating SLC8A1-AS1 expression and inactivating the pathway, ultimately suppressing proliferation in OC. Conclusions This study identifies SLC8A1-AS1 as a novel prognostic biomarker in OC and provides the first evidence that DHT exerts its antitumor effects by targeting the SRSF1/SLC8A1-AS1/FOXO1 axis. These findings unveil the role of SLC8A1-AS1 in OC progression and elucidate the mechanistic basis for the therapeutic potential of DHT.

title: Herbal bioactive compounds modulating ferroptosis and pyroptosis in neonatal hypoxic-ischemic brain injury: a systematic review of molecular basis, proposed crosstalk, and translational challenges
abstract: BACKGROUND: Neonatal hypoxic-ischemic brain injury (HIBI) remains a major cause of neonatal mortality and disability despite therapeutic hypothermia. Ferroptosis and pyroptosis are implicated in HIBI. PURPOSE: To critically evaluate herbal bioactive compounds modulating ferroptosis- and pyroptosis-associated injury in neonatal HIBI. STUDY DESIGN: Systematic review conducted and reported following PRISMA 2020. METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched through September 2026. Eligible studies used in vivo neonatal HIBI models, tested chemically defined plant-derived compounds, reported ferroptosis-related markers or evidence of pyroptotic execution beyond inflammasome activation, and assessed neuroprotective outcomes. Risk of bias was assessed using SYRCLE. RESULTS: Of 1441 records, 17 studies investigating 16 compounds met eligibility criteria. Nine examined ferroptosis and eight examined pyroptosis; glycyrrhizin was the only compound studied across both pathways, in separate studies. Included compounds spanned diverse structural classes and botanical sources. Studies reported reduced pathway-associated markers and improved brain-injury outcomes, but in vivo pathway dependency was demonstrated for only four compounds. No included study reported both ferroptosis-specific and pyroptosis-specific markers in the same neonatal HIBI model. Several risk-of-bias domains were predominantly rated unclear. CONCLUSION: Preclinical studies suggest that herbal bioactives can modulate ferroptosis- and pyroptosis-associated processes in neonatal HIBI and warrant further evaluation as multi-target candidates. However, no study tested whether a single compound modulates both pathways within the same model. Future studies should apply pathway-specific manipulation alongside assessment of the second pathway in the same model and address developmental-stage specificity, therapeutic timing, model variability, brain availability, formulation barriers, and other pharmacological considerations.

title: Modulatory effects of marine algae-derived natural products on nervous system
abstract: BACKGROUND: The pathological changes in neurodegenerative diseases are complicated and involve oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, protein misfolding, and synaptic loss. Marine algae contain a wide range of diverse natural compounds, such as polysaccharides, phenolics, terpenoids, and pigments, some of which may help preserve neurons by targeting oxidative pathways, dampening inflammatory responses, and preventing toxic protein aggregation. PURPOSE: This review aims to recapitulate current advances on the regulatory roles of marine algae-derived natural products on nervous system. In addition, representative compounds are discussed, together with the relationship between their structures and neuroprotective properties. METHODS: To conduct this structured narrative review, we collected relevant literature obtained from PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar up to June 2026. Relevant studies on the effect of algal products on neuroprotection were selected and articles were searched using terms that covered marine algae, natural products, neurodegenerative diseases, and structure-activity relationship. RESULTS: Natural products found in marine algae may support neuronal protection through the modulation of redox balance, inflammatory signaling, and proteostasis. Their neuroprotective activities are closely associated with structural determinants, and are intrinsically shaped by characteristics like sulfation degree, molecular weight, hydroxyl groups, and conjugated systems. CONCLUSION: This article underscores the potential of these products for neuroprotective interventions, and further studies are warranted to clarify their bioavailability and clinical efficacy.

title: A multifunctional Dendrobium officinale polysaccharide hydrogel loaded with propolis extract to promote oral mucosal repair
abstract: Oral ulcer is a prevalent mucosal injury characterized by bacterial infection, oxidative stress, and dysregulated inflammation, while current therapies remain insufficient to comprehensively regulate the complex healing process. Herein, we developed a multifunctional bioactive hydrogel (DH@Pro) by incorporating propolis extract into a dynamic polysaccharide network composed of Dendrobium officinale polysaccharide and phenylboronic acid-grafted hyaluronic acid HA-PBA. The DH@Pro hydrogel exhibited excellent antioxidant, immunomodulatory, regenerative properties and promoted angiogenesis. In vivo studies using rat oral ulcer models demonstrated that DH@Pro exerted distinct effects throughout different healing phases to achieve comprehensive oral ulcer repair. Furthermore, its therapeutic efficacy in a full-thickness skin wound model highlighted its broader regenerative potential. This study presents a natural polysaccharide-based hydrogel strategy that integrates infection control, inflammation regulation, and regeneration promotion for comprehensive oral ulcer repair.

title: Adjunctive fucoidan, fucoxanthin, and l-carnitine mitigate albuminuria and preserve eGFR over a 12-week treatment period in diabetic kidney disease: A translational study and proof-of-concept randomized clinical trial
abstract: Background and aim Standard therapies for diabetic kidney disease (DKD) reduce albuminuria but trigger an acute eGFR decline, limiting clinical initiation. We evaluated whether a standardized marine formula comprising oligo-fucoidan, fucoxanthin, and l-carnitine (FFL) provides potential renoprotective effects with stable renal function. Methods Preclinically, diabetic CKD mice received FFL for 8 weeks. Clinically, a 12-week randomized trial evaluated adjunctive FFL in DKD patients receiving SGLT2 inhibitors (100%) and ACEIs/ARBs (85.5%). Efficacy was analyzed using baseline-adjusted robust ANCOVA (per-protocol, n = 55) and validated under intention-to-treat (ITT, n = 63) sensitivity analysis with Baseline Observation Carried Forward imputation. Results Preclinically, FFL significantly attenuated renal dysfunction, tubulointerstitial fibrosis, and inflammation. Clinically, baseline-adjusted robust ANCOVA showed that adjunctive FFL achieved a highly significant, adjusted 39.40% greater reduction in UACR compared to control (Geometric Mean Ratio [GMR] = 0.60; 95% CI: 0.40-0.90; p = 0.01), which was validated under ITT-ANCOVA sensitivity analysis (adjusted 32.18% greater UACR reduction; GMR = 0.67; 95% CI: 0.48-0.93; p = 0.01). Crucially, eGFR remained stable and preserved over 12 weeks (PP adjusted GMR = 1.01, p = 0.74; ITT adjusted GMR = 1.01, p = 0.78). FFL also significantly lowered baseline-adjusted LDL (GMR = 0.85; 95% CI: 0.76-0.95; p Conclusion Standardized marine FFL is a safe, well-tolerated adjunctive therapy that reduces albuminuria and dyslipidemia while preserving stable renal hemodynamics over 12 weeks.

title: Hydroxytyrosol targets stemness and enhances chemotherapeutic response in 3D metastatic colorectal cancer spheroids
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cancer stem cells (CSCs) are increasingly recognized as critical mediators of tumour progression, recurrence and treatment resistance in metastatic colorectal cancer (CRC). Hydroxytyrosol, a phenolic compound derived from virgin olive oil, has shown promising anticancer activity against CRC cells. However, its effects on cancer stemness and its potential to enhance the efficacy of conventional chemotherapy drugs remain largely unexplored. PURPOSE: To assess whether hydroxytyrosol suppresses CSC-associated traits and improves chemotherapy response using a 3D spheroid model established from the metastatic CRC cell line LoVo. METHODS: LoVo spheroids were generated under stirred-tank culture conditions and characterized by molecular and functional assays. Hydroxytyrosol effects on LoVo spheroids were assessed using cell viability, ALDH activity, clonogenic and RT-qPCR assays. Drug combination interactions were determined using the Chou-Talalay method. RESULTS: : 1454 µM vs 91 µM). Hydroxytyrosol significantly decreased ALDH activity at 125-500 µM (39-57%) and clonogenic potential at 1-100 µM (21-84%). It also significantly affected the expression of markers associated with the proliferation (CDKN1A), epithelial-mesenchymal transition (VIM), Wnt/β-catenin (AXIN2) and stemness (CD44, CD133 and LGR5). In combination studies, hydroxytyrosol showed strong synergistic interactions with the chemotherapy drug irinotecan (Combination Index: 0.07-0.15). Similar effects were observed in CSC-enriched HT29 spheroids. CONCLUSION: This study provides the first evidence that hydroxytyrosol targets CRC CSC-associated phenotypes and synergistically enhances irinotecan efficacy in metastatic CRC spheroids. These findings position hydroxytyrosol as a promising adjuvant strategy to counteract CSC-associated drug resistance and sensitize metastatic CRC cells to chemotherapy, supporting its further evaluation as a chemosensitising agent in advanced CRC.

title: 3,4-dehydro-3‑hydroxy-α-lapachone, a novel naphthoquinone, ameliorates hepatic fibrosis by targeting the guanine nucleotide-binding protein G(i) subunit alpha-2/peroxiredoxin 1 signaling axis
abstract: Background Hepatic fibrosis progresses to irreversible cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma without timely clinical intervention. Despite substantial clinical burden, no targeted therapies are currently approved specifically for hepatic fibrosis across the broad spectrum of chronic liver diseases, leaving a critical unmet need. Verbena officinalis L. has long been used in traditional medicine for hepatobiliary disorders, yet its active constituents, molecular targets, and mechanisms of antifibrotic action remain largely uncharacterized. Purpose This study was designed to identify novel anti-hepatic fibrosis components of Verbena officinalis and elucidate their underlying mechanisms of action. Methods Therapeutic efficacy was assessed in bile duct ligation and carbon tetrachloride-induced liver fibrosis mouse models. Bioactivity-guided fractionation coupled with high-content screening was applied to isolate active metabolites. Drug affinity responsive target stability identified candidate targets; direct binding was validated via surface plasmon resonance, cellular thermal shift assay, and molecular docking. Mechanisms were confirmed through integrated molecular and functional studies. Results The ethyl acetate fraction exhibited the most potent anti-hepatic fibrotic activity, from which thirty-four metabolites, including two previously undescribed naphthoquinones (1 and 2) and one new dammarane-type triterpenoid (16), were isolated. Compound 1, identified as 3,4-dehydro-3‑hydroxy-α-lapachone (DH), demonstrated robust anti-fibrotic efficacy. Notably, DH at 10 mg/kg achieved in vivo efficacy comparable to the clinical agent pirfenidone at 200 mg/kg under the tested experimental conditions. Mechanistically, DH directly binds guanine nucleotide-binding protein G(i) subunit alpha-2 (GNAI2) at residues Phe171 and Leu250, suppressing the GNAI2-peroxiredoxin 1 (PRDX1) signaling axis to attenuate fibrogenesis. GNAI2 is consistently associated with fibrotic progression across multiple disease contexts and acts as an important functional mediator of hepatic stellate cell activation and hepatic fibrosis. Conclusion This work establishes DH as an anti-fibrotic agent with a rigorously validated protein target and binding mechanism, addressing a longstanding translational gap in phytochemical research. DH acts primarily through GNAI2-PRDX1 pathway inhibition. We acknowledge that DH possesses well-described redox-active properties and may therefore engage additional intracellular targets; accordingly, the GNAI2-PRDX1 axis represents the primary validated mediator rather than the exclusive mechanism of action. These findings establish GNAI2 as a novel therapeutic target and identify DH as a promising lead compound for the development of novel anti-fibrotic agents.

title: Tangeretin alleviates airway hyperresponsiveness through epithelial prostaglandin E2 signaling
Metabolic conversion of dioscin-diosgenin and their interactions with gut microbiota: recent advances
