abstract: Background HMF plants are rich sources of steroidal saponins, and dioscin and diosgenin are the widely distributed and bioactive compounds. Despite their poor oral bioavailability, these saponins undergo extensive microbial transformation, yielding bioavailable metabolites with enhanced lipophilicity and pharmacological potential. Recent studies indicate that the interaction between diosgenin and the gut microbiota plays a crucial role in regulating metabolic, immune, and neuroendocrine functions. Understanding this bidirectional relationship may provide a foundation for developing novel microbiota-targeted nutritional and therapeutic strategies. Purpose The purpose of this review was to summarize current research progress on the biotransformation, biological functions, and health implications of diosgenin and its precursors. We elucidate how microbial metabolism modulates diosgenin activity and how diosgenin reshapes gut microbial composition and function to maintain intestinal homeostasis. Methods A comprehensive literature search was conducted using four major electronic databases, including PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and CNKI, were searched from inception to January 2026. Key words used in the literature search were "diosgenin", "dioscin", "steroidal saponins", "gut microbiota", "homology of medicine and food", "β-glucosidase", "microbial transformation", "mucosal immunity", "metabolic and inflammatory disorders" and "gut brain axis". Keywords are linked with AND/OR. Chemical structure data and biotransformation pathways were confirmed through peer-reviewed sources and authoritative databases such as NIH and PubChem. Results Evidence indicates that intestinal microbial β-glucosidases catalyze the deglycosylation of dioscin into lipophilic aglycone diosgenin, thereby enhancing its membrane permeability and bioactivity. Diosgenin selectively enriches beneficial microbial populations and promotes the production of key microbial metabolites, including SCFAs and tryptophan-derived indoles. These microbial metabolites play pivotal roles in intestinal epithelial integrity and mucosal immune homeostasis. They modulate the Treg balance by activating key host signaling pathways. The primary receptors involved include GPRs, AHR, and PPARs. Preclinical studies strongly support the therapeutic potential of the microbiota-diosgenin axis in alleviating T2D, NAFLD, IBD, neuroinflammation, and age-related pathologies. Conclusion This review highlights the gut microbiota as an important modulator of diosgenin bioavailability and biological activity, based largely on preclinical evidence. Differences in microbial composition and metabolic capacity may contribute to interindividual variability in host responses to diosgenin. In this context, we propose the concept of diosgenin metabotypes as a conceptual framework to describe microbiota-dependent differences in diosgenin metabolism, which may inform future microbiome-guided nutritional and therapeutic strategies.

title: Qishen Yangxin Granule ameliorates cardiac function and ventricular remodeling in dilated cardiomyopathy by attenuating inflammation and myocardial fibrosis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Qishen Yangxin Granule (QSYX), a clinically utilized traditional Chinese medicinal formula, has demonstrated therapeutic efficacy for cardiovascular diseases. However, its cardioprotective mechanism in dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) remains incompletely defined. PURPOSE: To evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of QSYX against DCM and the associated anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic mechanisms. METHODS: Cardioprotective effects of QSYX were assessed both in vivo using a doxorubicin-induced DCM rat model and in vitro using rat cardiac fibroblasts stimulated with lipopolysaccharide. Evaluations included cardiac function, histopathological analysis, levels of inflammatory factors, and myocardial fibrosis markers. Single-cell RNA sequencing was employed to explore the potential mechanism of QSYX-mediated improvement in cardiac structure and function. Modulation of the toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (p38 MAPK)/nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) pathway was examined via western blot, immunohistochemistry, confocal laser scanning microscope, and real-time reverse transcription-PCR. The specific p38 MAPK agonist LY188011 was used to verify the dependence of QSYX effect on the TLR4/p38 MAPK/NF-κB signaling pathway. RESULTS: QSYX administration improved cardiac function in DCM rats, accompanied by significant attenuation of cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, apoptosis, inflammatory cell infiltration, and collagen deposition. Comparable protective effects were observed in lipopolysaccharide-treated cardiac fibroblasts. Mechanistically, QSYX suppressed lipopolysaccharide-induced upregulation of TLR4, p38 MAPK, and NF-κB p65 and downregulated the expression of inflammatory factors and myocardial fibrosis markers. Furthermore, intervention with LY188011 confirmed that the cardioprotective effects of QSYX are mediated through suppression of the TLR4/p38 MAPK/NF-κB signaling pathway. CONCLUSION: QSYX attenuates myocardial inflammation and fibrosis primarily through inhibition of the TLR4/p38 MAPK/NF-κB signaling pathway, thereby exerting cardioprotective effects against DCM-induced cardiac injury.

title: Activity of the natural biflavonoid hinokiflavone against multidrug-resistant CEM/ADR5000 leukemia cells and its modes of action via P-glycoprotein modulation
abstract: Background Multidrug resistance (MDR), frequently associated with the overexpression of ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters such as P-glycoprotein (P-gp), is a major obstacle to successful leukemia chemotherapy. Natural products represent an important source for anticancer drug discovery. Hinokiflavone, a natural biflavonoid, has demonstrated anticancer potential, but its underlying mechanisms against multidrug-resistant leukemia are largely unknown. Hypothesis We hypothesized that hinokiflavone exhibits preferential activity against P-gp-overexpressing multidrug-resistant leukemia cells through specific mechanisms associated with the multidrug-resistant phenotype. Methods Cytotoxicity was evaluated in parental and drug-resistant cell models, and the contribution of ABCB1/P-gp to the collateral sensitivity of CEM/ADR5000 cells was investigated by siRNA-mediated ABCB1 knockdown. Molecular docking was performed to predict potential interactions with both P-gp and breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP). mRNA-based transcriptomic expression profiling, Western blot analysis, pathway analyses, and siRNA-mediated TXNIP knockdown were used to investigate signaling alterations. Intracellular ROS generation, mitochondrial membrane potential, P-gp-associated drug transport, ATP levels, cell cycle distribution, DNA damage, and apoptosis were further investigated. In addition, a zebrafish xenograft model was used to evaluate preliminary in vivo antitumor activity. Results Hinokiflavone exhibited collateral sensitivity toward P-gp-overexpressing CEM/ADR5000 leukemia cells, and ABCB1 knockdown markedly reduced this sensitivity. Moreover, hinokiflavone significantly restored doxorubicin sensitivity in multidrug-resistant CEM/ADR5000 cells, reducing the IC₅₀ of doxorubicin by 3.17-fold, comparable to the P-glycoprotein inhibitor verapamil. Molecular docking predicted interactions with both P-gp and BCRP. Transcriptomic and protein analyses revealed alterations in several signaling pathways (activated WNT/β-catenin signaling, increased TXNIP and PTEN expression, and reduced PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling). TXNIP knockdown attenuated the effects of hinokiflavone on PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling and reduced the cytotoxic response. Hinokiflavone treatment was also associated with ROS accumulation, mitochondrial membrane depolarization, altered P-gp-associated drug transport, ATP depletion, G2/M-related cell-cycle alterations, DNA damage, and apoptosis. Hinokiflavone additionally exhibited preliminary antitumor activity in an SK-N-DZ zebrafish xenograft model. Conclusion Hinokiflavone exhibits collateral sensitivity in P-gp-overexpressing CEM/ADR5000 leukemia cells, with ABCB1/P-glycoprotein contributing substantially to this phenotype. Its activity is associated with oxidative stress, energy metabolism, P-gp-associated drug transport, and multiple survival signaling pathways. These findings highlight hinokiflavone’s potential for targeting multidrug-resistant leukemia.

title: Isoliquiritigenin attenuates doxorubicin-induced cardiomyopathy by alleviating mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage through the Piezo1/Ca²⁺/Pdk4 signaling axis
Eupalinolide B targets the USP10-AR-MTHFD1 axis to sensitize castration-resistant prostate cancer to enzalutamide
abstract: Background Acquired resistance to enzalutamide (ENZ) remains a major obstacle in the treatment of castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC). Although persistent androgen receptor (AR) signaling is a central determinant of limited responsiveness to ENZ, the post-translational mechanisms that maintain AR protein stability during ENZ treatment remain insufficiently understood. Purpose This study aimed to define the role of ubiquitin-specific protease 10 (USP10) in CRPC adaptive responses to ENZ treatment and determine whether Eupalinolide B (EB) could enhance ENZ sensitivity by targeting the USP10-AR-MTHFD1 axis. Methods CRPC cell models and xenograft mouse models were established to evaluate the effects of EB on ENZ sensitivity both in vitro and in vivo. Protein interaction and localization were analyzed using immunoprecipitation, binding assays and immunofluorescence. AR ubiquitination and degradation were evaluated by ubiquitination assays and proteasome inhibition experiments. Functional assays were performed to investigate the impact of EB on cell proliferation and tumor progression, and mechanistic studies were conducted to explore the involvement of the USP10-AR-MTHFD1 signaling axis. Results USP10 translocated to the nucleus under ENZ treatment and contributed to reduced ENZ responsiveness in CRPC. EB disrupted the USP10-AR interaction by targeting the catalytic domain of USP10, promoting ubiquitination-mediated AR degradation, and suppressing the downstream AR-MTHFD1 axis. Consequently, EB enhanced the antitumor efficacy of ENZ against CRPC both in vitro and in vivo. Conclusion USP10 is a potential therapeutic vulnerability in CRPC, and EB represents a promising lead compound for ENZ-based combination therapy.

title: Multiscale and Cross-Organ Antidiabetic Effects of Ajuga decumbens and Harpagide: Integrating Hepatic Metabolism, Immune Regulation, and Gut Microbiota
Jingfang granule alleviates cold-damp lung injury by suppressing NF-κB/HIF-1α-associated macrophage glycolysis
abstract: Background Jingfang Granule (JFG) is clinically used for exterior cold-damp disorders, but its pulmonary effects and associated inflammatory responses remain incompletely understood. Purpose To evaluate the protective effects of JFG against cold-damp syndrome-like lung injury and its effects on macrophage glycolytic inflammatory activation. Study design A combined in vivo, multi-omics and in vitro mechanistic study was conducted. Methods Rats were exposed to low-temperature/high-humidity conditions and treated with JFG. Lung pathology, inflammatory responses, targeted serum energy metabolomics, matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization mass spectrometry imaging (MALDI-MSI), transcriptomics and proteomics were evaluated. UPLC fingerprinting and UPLC-Q-TOF-MS/MS-based serum pharmacochemistry were used to characterize JFG and its absorbed constituents. LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages were treated with JFG-medicated serum. DMOG rescue, HIF-1α knockdown, BAY 11-7082-mediated NF-κB inhibition, fluorometric ECAR assay and representative-compound validation were performed to strengthen mechanistic interpretation. Results JFG improved cold-damp-related phenotypes, reduced pulmonary edema, mucus hypersecretion, inflammatory cytokine levels and CD68/iNOS-positive macrophage accumulation. Metabolomics and MALDI-MSI showed that JFG corrected glycolysis- and TCA cycle-related disturbances. Integrated multi-omics highlighted the NF-κB/HIF-1α-HK2/LDHA pathway as a major JFG-regulated axis. In LPS-stimulated macrophages, JFG-medicated serum reduced glycolysis-associated markers and CD86-positive M1-like activation. DMOG partially reversed these effects, whereas HIF-1α knockdown reduced HK2, LDHA, iNOS expression and extracellular acidification, weakening the additional inhibitory effect of JFG-medicated serum. BAY 11-7082 further supported the involvement of NF-κB in HIF-1α-associated glycolytic activation. Prim-O-glucosylcimifugin (POG), nobiletin and quercetin partially reproduced the inhibitory effects of JFG-medicated serum on pathway-associated proteins in vitro. Conclusion JFG attenuated cold-damp syndrome-like lung injury in rats, accompanied by improvements in pulmonary inflammation and glycolysis-related metabolic disturbances. Complementary experiments in LPS-stimulated macrophages supported the involvement of NF-κB/HIF-1α-associated glycolytic activation in the anti-inflammatory effects of JFG-medicated serum, while serum pharmacochemistry provided evidence of absorbed constituents.

title: Puerarin preserves microglial homeostasis and protects against acute cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury by regulating autophagy and oxidative stress through Janus kinase 2/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3
abstract: Background Microglial oxidative stress and dysregulated autophagy contribute to secondary neuronal injury following ischemic stroke. Puerarin (PUE), a bioactive isoflavone with established antioxidative and neuroprotective properties, may protect against cerebral ischemia by modulating microglial dysfunction; however, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Methods The neuroprotective effects of PUE were investigated in a rat transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO) model and in BV2 microglia subjected to oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R). Microglial phenotypic alterations, oxidative stress, and autophagic activity were evaluated using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), ultrastructural, biochemical, and fluorescence-based analyses. Data-independent acquisition (DIA) proteomics, pharmacological gain- and loss-of-function approaches, and adeno-associated virus serotype 9 (AAV9)-mediated Janus kinase 2 ( JAK2 ) knockdown were employed to define the role of Janus kinase 2/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (JAK2/STAT3) signaling. Microglia-mediated neuroprotection was further assessed using an HT22 neuron–microglia co-culture system. Results PUE reshaped the microglial landscape by preserving the homeostatic microglial phenotype while suppressing ischemia-induced pathological activation. PUE reduced intracellular and mitochondrial ROS production, restored redox homeostasis, suppressed excessive autophagosome formation, and downregulated the autophagy-related proteins 3/5/12 (ATG3/5/12). Mechanistically, these protective effects were mediated through inhibition of JAK2/STAT3 signaling. Genetic silencing of JAK2 recapitulated the effects of PUE, whereas pharmacological activation of JAK2/STAT3 largely abolished its antioxidative, anti-autophagic, and neuroprotective activities. Furthermore, conditioned media from PUE-treated microglia significantly alleviated neuronal injury in HT22 cells, supporting a microglia-mediated paracrine mechanism of neuroprotection. Conclusion Collectively, these findings identify JAK2/STAT3-dependent regulation of the oxidative stress-autophagy axis as a critical mechanism underlying microglial homeostasis after acute cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) and establish PUE as a promising therapeutic candidate for ischemic stroke.

title: Identification of cepharanthine as a novel senolytic that selectively eliminates senescent cells by regulating cell survival signaling pathways
abstract: BACKGROUND: Senolytics are small-molecule drugs that selectively induce apoptosis in senescent cells, thereby reducing the chronic inflammation and tissue damage caused by the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) and delaying aging, improving organ function and extending healthspan. Existing senolytics, however, often suffer from low bioavailability and off-target toxicity, so potent and safer senolytics are urgently needed. PURPOSE: To screen for novel senolytic compounds and validate the ability of cepharanthine (CEP) to eliminate senescent cells, improve organ function and extend lifespan. STUDY DESIGN: Preclinical study combining in vitro phenotypic screening and mechanistic assays with in vivo validation in zebrafish, C. elegans, naturally aged mice and a Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) mouse model. METHODS: Senolytic efficacy was assessed by a senescent cell-based phenotypic screen, IC₅₀ determination, inhibitor-based rescue assays and multiple senescence models. RNA-seq and pathway enrichment identified the key PI3K/AKT and PERK-ATF4-CHOP pathways, verified by Western blot, qRT-PCR, immunofluorescence and mitochondrial assays. In vivo efficacy was evaluated by senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) staining, HE staining, immunofluorescence, ELISA, biochemical assays and survival analysis. RESULTS: CEP selectively eliminates senescent cells by cooperatively and in parallel regulating the PI3K/AKT and PERK-ATF4-CHOP pathways, differentially inducing PUMA/NOXA and triggering mitochondrial intrinsic apoptosis. In zebrafish, C. elegans, naturally aged mice and HGPS mice, CEP clears senescent cells, reduces SASP levels, improves organ function and prolongs lifespan. CONCLUSION: CEP is a novel natural senolytic that induces mitochondrial intrinsic apoptosis via parallel, non-redundant regulation of the PI3K/AKT and PERK-ATF4-CHOP pathways, showing good potential for clinical translation.

title: Omega-3 PUFAs in the prevention of radiation-induced esophagitis
abstract: Background and Aim Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) have anti-inflammatory and tissue-protective properties. This study aimed to investigate the role and potential mechanism of PUFAs in preventing acute radiation esophagitis (ARE). Methods A murine ARE model was established, and multi-omics analyses, including proteomics, metabolomics, and single-cell RNA sequencing, were performed as well as in vitro experiments using human esophageal epithelial cells. A retrospective clinical analysis was performed to evaluate the effects of deep-sea fish oil (FO) containing omega-3 PUFAs. Results In the mouse ARE model, esophagus proteomic analysis revealed that, compared with irradiation (IR), IR + docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) resulted in greater enrichment of proteins in the mitochondrial inner membrane and oxidative phosphorylation pathways. Furthermore, metabolomics revealed significantly reduced levels of radiation-induced metabolic products such as Cer 17:1;2O/16:0;(2OH), Cer 18:0;3O/16:0, LPC 40:7, lactobionic acid, and pantetheine after IR, and the addition of DHA significantly reversed these changes. In human esophageal epithelial cells (HEECs), omega-3 PUFAs mitigated irradiation-induced mitochondrial damage by modulating respiratory chain proteins, reducing intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels and enhancing cell viability. Single-cell RNA sequencing showed that DHA addition reshaped intercellular communication and inflammatory signaling, and also modulated the cell fate trajectories of fibroblasts and endothelial cells in irradiated mouse esophageal tissues. Our retrospective investigation found that FO supplementation significantly reduced ARE severity (odds ratio=0.36, P =0.006) and pain scores ( P =0.018) in esophageal cancer patients undergoing radiotherapy compared with those in patients receiving radiotherapy alone. Conclusion Omega-3 PUFAs can prevent ARE mainly by regulating mitochondrial metabolism, intercellular communication networks, inflammatory signaling, and the fate trajectories of fibroblasts and endothelial cells. The potential anti-ARE effect of FO requires more clinical trials for verification.

title: Therapeutic effects and mechanisms of betaine on airway inflammation in severe asthma
abstract: Background Severe asthma in children is often complicated by glucocorticoid resistance, which limits the efficacy of standard anti-inflammatory therapy. Given its potent anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, betaine emerges as a promising candidate to mitigate airway inflammation and warrants targeted investigation. Methods We employed metabolomics and transcriptomics to identify differential plasma metabolites and genes in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from children experiencing acute severe asthma attacks. The impact of betaine was evaluated in a severe asthma mouse model induced by ovalbumin (OVA) and lipopolysaccharide (LPS). The impact on inflammation was assessed by treating BEAS-2B cells with IL-17A, both in the presence and absence of betaine. To elucidate the underlying mechanisms, Salvador family protein 1 (SAV1) knockdown and overexpression experiments were conducted, followed by qRT-PCR, Western blotting, and immunofluorescence analyses. Results Differential plasma metabolites of children with severe asthma were mainly concentrated in glycine, serine, and threonine metabolic pathway. Betaine, which is the key metabolite, was downregulated in the asthma group. Genes regulating betaine metabolism were downregulated in PBMCs from children with severe asthma. Betaine decreased both total white blood cell counts and neutrophil percentages in the bronchoalveolar lavage fluids (BALFs) of mice with OVA and LPS stimulation. It also alleviated lung inflammation, mucus hypersecretion, and collagen fiber deposition. Although betaine did not reduce Th17 cell numbers or IL‑17A secretion in lung tissues, it decreased the levels of IL‑1β, IL‑6, and CXCL8 in both BALFs and lung tissues. In BEAS‑2B cells, betaine attenuated IL‑17A induced IL‑6 and CXCL8 release. Mechanistically, these effects may involve activation of the Hippo pathway via SAV1, leading to increased YAP phosphorylation and reduced YAP nuclear translocation. Silencing SAV1 abolished betaine induced YAP cytoplasmic retention and reversed its anti-inflammatory effects. Conclusion Betaine alleviates airway inflammation in a severe asthma mouse model and reduces inflammatory mediator secretion by airway epithelial cells.

title: Machine Learning-Guided Multimodal Analysis of APAF1-Associated Tumor Microenvironment Features Prioritizes Macrocarpene A for Gastric Cancer
Atractylenolide III alleviates MASLD by inhibiting lipid synthesis and apoptosis via PTEN
Ginkgolide K restrains pulmonary fibrosis by disrupting a STING–FTH1 proteolytic ferroptosis axis
abstract: Background Pulmonary fibrosis (PF) is driven by persistent fibroblast activation and excessive extracellular matrix deposition. Stimulator of interferon genes (STING) has been implicated in tissue fibrosis, but whether it directly regulates ferroptosis and iron homeostasis in fibroblasts through noncanonical mechanisms remains unclear. Ginkgolide K (GinK), a bioactive diterpene trilactone from Ginkgo biloba , has antioxidant and immunomodulatory properties, but its role in PF is poorly understood. Purpose This study aimed to define the role of STING in ferroptosis-associated fibroblast activation and to determine whether GinK exerts antifibrotic effects by targeting this pathway. Study design and methods Bleomycin-induced PF was established in wild-type and STING-knockout mice, and TGF-β1-stimulated NIH/3T3 fibroblasts were used as an in vitro model. STING gain- and loss-of-function approaches were used to determine its role in fibroblast activation and ferroptosis. IP-MS, co-immunoprecipitation, ubiquitination assays, cycloheximide chase, and proteasome inhibition were performed to investigate the regulation of ferritin heavy chain 1 (FTH1) stability. Ferroptosis-associated changes were assessed by measuring intracellular Fe²⁺, lipid peroxidation, and related protein markers. Representative ginkgolide constituents were subsequently screened, and the pharmacological effects of GinK were evaluated in vitro and in vivo. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and experiments using a STING triple mutant were performed to examine GinK–STING binding and STING involvement in the cellular response to GinK. Results STING expression was increased in fibrotic lungs and activated fibroblasts. STING knockout attenuated BLM-induced pulmonary fibrosis, and STING silencing reduced fibroblast activation. STING promoted intracellular Fe²⁺ accumulation and lipid peroxidation, linking STING activation to ferroptotic stress. Mechanistically, STING associated with FTH1 and promoted its polyubiquitination and proteasome-dependent degradation without altering Fth1 mRNA levels. Loss of FTH1 disrupted iron homeostasis and enhanced ferroptosis-associated fibroblast activation. This effect was not reproduced by cGAMP stimulation and was not prevented by cGAS inhibition, supporting a noncanonical STING mechanism independent of upstream cGAS–cGAMP activation. Integrated proteomic and ubiquitination analyses further identified NEDD4 as a candidate E3 ligase involved in FTH1 turnover. Among the ginkgolide constituents screened, GinK showed the strongest predicted interaction with STING. GinK suppressed STING abundance, restored FTH1-mediated iron homeostasis, reduced ferroptotic stress and fibroblast activation, and attenuated bleomycin-induced PF. STING overexpression markedly weakened the protective effects of GinK. SPR demonstrated GinK–STING binding with a steady-state KD of 12.48 μM. GinK did not significantly reduce intracellular Fe²⁺ accumulation or lipid peroxidation in cells expressing the S161A/R237A/T262A STING mutant under the tested conditions. Conclusion GinK alleviates pulmonary fibrosis by suppressing a noncanonical STING–FTH1 pathway that promotes FTH1 degradation, iron dyshomeostasis, and ferroptosis-associated fibroblast activation. These findings support a mechanism linking STING to fibroblast ferroptosis and provide a mechanistic basis for the antifibrotic activity of GinK.

title: TSP promotes ferroptosis in breast cancer cells to suppress osteolytic bone metastasis
Ginsenoside Rg6 ameliorates COPD by targeting RAGE to suppress MAPK/NF-κB signaling, thereby preserving alveolar barrier integrity and attenuating EMT
abstract: Abstract：Background: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is pathologically characterized by progressive alveolar epithelial barrier disruption, a pathological process primarily driven by chronic cigarette smoke exposure. While Ginsenoside Rg6 (Rg6) has shown therapeutic promise in pulmonary injury models, its direct molecular targets and the precise mechanisms by which it preserves barrier integrity remain unclear.Purpose: This study investigates whether Rg6 mitigates COPD by directly targeting the RAGE receptor, thereby suppressing the downstream signaling axes concurrently preserve alveolar barrier integrity and attenuate epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT).Methods: The therapeutic efficacy of Rg6 was evaluated in CSE-challenged MLE-12 alveolar epithelial cells and an LPS/CS-driven mouse COPD model. Transcriptomic profiling was utilized to identify upstream regulatory nodes. Direct Rg6-RAGE engagement was rigorously validated via molecular docking, MD simulations, surface plasmon resonance (SPR), DARTS, and CETSA. The functional dependency of Rg6's protective effects on RAGE was dissected using siRNA knockdown in vitro and AAV-shRAGE delivery in vivo.Results: Oral Rg6 significantly ameliorated pulmonary function decline, emphysema, and the inflammatory microenvironment in COPD mice, achieving efficacy comparable to dexamethasone. Crucially, Rg6 effectively preserved alveolar barrier integrity, restored tight junctions, and attenuated EMT-associated phenotypic shifts. Transcriptomic profiling identified the AGE-RAGE axis as the central upstream hub governing this structural protection. Comprehensive biophysical assays confirmed that Rg6 directly binds to and thermodynamically stabilizes the RAGE protein pocket. Mechanistically, Rg6 suppressed RAGE-mediated hyperactivation of the MAPK (p38, JNK) and NF-κB (p65) cascades, which serve as the central drivers for tight junction disassembly and EMT in epithelial cells. Furthermore, RAGE ablation in vitro and in vivo demonstrated that Rg6's capacity to preserve epithelial architecture is primarily RAGE-dependent.Conclusions: Rg6 directly targets alveolar RAGE to inhibit the RAGE-MAPK/NF-κB signaling cascade. By suppressing this axis, Rg6 concurrently preserves alveolar barrier integrity and attenuates EMT-like transitions, actively restoring alveolar structural homeostasis and positioning it as a promising disease-modifying candidate for COPD.
